questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Respiratory quotient: a ratio is not an identification
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: A fictional teacher dataset shows that germinating seeds used 45.0 cm3 of oxygen while producing 36.0 cm3 of carbon dioxide during the same observation interval. Assume both readings were corrected to comparable temperature and pressure.
tasks: Calculate the respiratory quotient, with its unit status.
Explain what this value suggests about the respiratory substrate.
Identify two reasons why the measurement does not uniquely identify the substrate.
marks: RQ = CO2 volume / O2 volume for the same time interval.
RQ is dimensionless when comparable volumes are used.
An RQ below 1 is consistent with relatively oxygen-demanding oxidation, for example fat-rich respiration.
It does not prove that only fats were respired.
Mixed substrates can produce intermediate quotients.
Gas exchange or dissolution and measurement limitations can bias a sampled RQ.
The volumes must be compared under equivalent temperature and pressure.
questions.common_error: Infering a unique organic substrate solely from RQ.
questions.transfer_question: For another hypothetical data pair, CO2=30.0 cm3 and O2=40.0 cm3. Find RQ and state what cannot be concluded.
questions.transfer_answer: 0.750; it does not uniquely identify the substrate.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Potometer data: uptake is not identical to transpiration
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies hypothetical observations from a very narrow capillary: inner radius 0.250 mm, bubble displacement 80.0 mm in 5.00 min. Assume a circular cross-section and no change in tube radius.
tasks: Calculate the volume of water movement and rate in mm3 min-1.
Express the rate in microlitres per minute.
Explain why this need not equal actual transpiration at that instant.
marks: Volume = area x distance = 0.19635 x 80.0 = 15.7 mm3.
1 mm3 = 1 microlitre, so rate = 3.14 microlitres min-1.
The measured variable is capillary water uptake (a proxy).
Some water can be used or stored in tissues.
Environmental conditions can change water loss during measurement.
Measurement uncertainty in radius is magnified by the squared-radius term.
questions.common_error: Treating the water-uptake proxy as a direct, universally equal measurement of transpiration.
questions.transfer_question: If the measured inner radius is doubled while bubble speed is unchanged, by what factor does inferred flow change?
questions.transfer_answer: Factor of four: volume rate is proportional to cross-sectional area, and area is proportional to r2.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Electron-image scale: recalibrate after resizing
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: On an illustrative printed micrograph, a scale bar representing 40.0 micrometres measures 20.0 mm on the page. An organelle on that same image spans 7.50 mm. The worksheet was not calibrated to a real specimen.
tasks: Calculate the enlargement of this particular printed image.
Estimate the represented organelle length.
State why the displayed page enlargement is not an intrinsic property of the original specimen.
marks: 20.0 mm = 20,000 micrometres.
Image enlargement = 20,000 / 40.0 = 500 times.
The scale ratio is 40.0 micrometres / 20.0 mm = 2.00 micrometres per mm.
Organelle represented length = 7.50 x 2.00 = 15.0 micrometres.
Units of bar and image length must be converted before division.
Resizing a document changes the printed enlargement.
Resizing both scale bar and image together preserves the inferred specimen size.
A calibration bar is more reliable than claiming a fixed enlargement after a rescaled export.
questions.common_error: Reading a printed enlargement from a rescaled image without recalibration.
questions.transfer_question: If the entire image is enlarged to twice its printed dimensions, what is the new printed enlargement and the inferred organelle length?
questions.transfer_answer: 1,000 times and still 15.0 micrometres, provided the scale bar enlarges with the image.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Plasmolysis threshold: interpolation is an estimate
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: A fictional slide-count dataset reports 20% of cells classified as plasmolysed at 0.20 mol dm-3 and 55% at 0.30 mol dm-3. No observations were made between these two concentrations.
tasks: Find the concentration estimated to give 50% plasmolysis by linear interpolation.
Explain why the answer is not an exact experimental concentration.
State what extra information is needed to infer solute potential.
marks: Difference in proportion = 55 - 20 = 35 percentage points.
Needed rise from 20% to 50% is 30 percentage points.
Interpolation fraction = 30/35 = 6/7.
Estimated concentration = 0.20 + (6/7)(0.10) = 0.2857 mol dm-3.
Round appropriately: about 0.286 mol dm-3.
The estimate assumes approximately linear behaviour in this interval.
Cell classification and sampling variation require uncertainty or more points.
Solute potential needs temperature, effective solute-particle concentration and a justified physicochemical model; concentration alone is not a reported potential.
questions.common_error: Reporting an interpolated 50% level as though it was directly measured or universally fixed.
questions.transfer_question: At 0.20 mol dm-3 35% are plasmolysed, at 0.30 mol dm-3 60%. Estimate the 50% threshold.
questions.transfer_answer: 0.20 + (15/25) x 0.10 = 0.260 mol dm-3 under linear interpolation.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Molar-volume reasoning at stated reference conditions
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: For a fictional ideal-gas dataset, take P = 99.6 kPa, V = 250 cm3, T = 300 K. Use R = 8.314 J mol-1 K-1. Ignore real-gas and water-vapour corrections for this model.
tasks: Determine the amount of gas, in mol.
Estimate its ideal volume at 273.15 K and 101.325 kPa.
Explain why the measured 250 cm3 is not the gas molar volume.
marks: Use n = PV/(RT).
At the chosen reference state Vref = n R Tref / Pref.
Vref is about 0.000224 m3 = 0.224 dm3 for this quantity of gas.
Molar volume refers to volume per mole at specified reference conditions, not a raw sample volume.
Units and assumptions (ideal gas, same gas amount) must be stated; real-gas and water-vapour effects are omitted.
questions.common_error: Misidentifying a sample volume as a volume per mole, or using kPa and cm3 with SI R without conversions.
questions.transfer_question: For a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant pressure, V=200 cm3 at 300 K. Predict V at 330 K.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Calorimetry: heat gained versus reaction enthalpy
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: An already-completed fictional teacher dataset reports a 50.0 g solution warming from 22.5 C to 28.0 C. Use c=4.18 J g-1 K-1 and 0.0250 mol of reaction as defined by its stoichiometric extent. Suppose a hypothetical calorimeter heat capacity is 45.0 J K-1.
tasks: Calculate the heat gained by the solution.
Calculate the inferred molar reaction enthalpy first neglecting, then including, the calorimeter heat capacity.
Explain one remaining cause of underestimating the exothermic magnitude.
marks: Temperature rise = 28.0 - 22.5 = 5.5 K.
Solution heat = mc DeltaT = 50.0 x 4.18 x 5.5 = 1.15 kJ.
Neglecting calorimeter, reaction DeltaH = -1.1495/0.0250 = -46.0 kJ mol-1.
Calorimeter heat = 45.0 x 5.5 = 247.5 J.
Combined heat gained = 1397 J.
Including calorimeter, DeltaH = -1397/0.0250 = -55.9 kJ mol-1.
The minus sign indicates exothermic reaction under the stated model.
Energy lost to surroundings before observation of the peak is not included and can further underestimate the magnitude.
questions.common_error: Equating heat gained by solution alone to total reaction heat without stating the calorimeter/loss assumptions.
questions.transfer_question: If the calorimeter heat capacity were 0, what would be the inferred DeltaH for this data?
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Concordant titres: transparency in selecting results
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: In a teacher-written 1:1 neutralisation model, the available titres are 24.22, 24.20, 24.24 and 25.00 cm3. The standard concentration is 0.1000 mol dm-3, the unknown aliquot is 25.00 cm3, and the classroom concordance criterion is a spread no greater than 0.10 cm3.
tasks: Identify the cluster and calculate its mean.
Under the stated 1:1 model, find the unknown concentration.
Explain how the discordant reading should be recorded.
marks: The 25.00 cm3 value lies outside the tight cluster and requires investigation.
24.20, 24.22 and 24.24 cm3 have a spread of 0.04 cm3.
Mean concordant titre = (24.20+24.22+24.24)/3 = 24.22 cm3.
Amount of standard = 0.1000 x 0.02422 = 0.002422 mol.
Amount of unknown = 0.002422 mol for the specified 1:1 equation.
Unknown concentration = 0.002422/0.02500 = 0.09688 mol dm-3.
The criterion and accepted trials must be disclosed, rather than silently hiding results.
Endpoint judgement and reading uncertainty limit significant claims about concentration.
questions.common_error: Deleting an inconvenient titre without reporting it or explaining the selection criterion.
questions.transfer_question: If a fictional 1:1 titre were 25.00 cm3 at 0.1000 mol dm-3 standard for a 20.00 cm3 aliquot, find unknown concentration.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Rate law from controlled comparisons and units
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: A model provides three independent initial-rate measurements with temperature and other conditions fixed: run 1 [A]=0.100 mol dm-3, [B]=0.100 mol dm-3, rate=0.00200 mol dm-3 s-1; run 2 [A]=0.200, [B]=0.100, rate=0.00800; run 3 [A]=0.100, [B]=0.200, rate=0.00400.
tasks: Infer the separate empirical orders in A and B.
Calculate the rate constant and its units.
Predict the rate at [A]=0.150 and [B]=0.200 mol dm-3.
marks: Doubling A at constant B multiplies rate by four.
Thus empirical order in A is 2 under the model.
Doubling B at constant A doubles rate.
Thus empirical order in B is 1 under the model.
Rate law: rate = k[A]^2[B].
Experimental order is not automatically the stoichiometric coefficient or a confirmed elementary mechanism.
questions.common_error: Equating reaction order with a balanced-equation coefficient without measured kinetic evidence.
questions.transfer_question: If [A] is tripled with [B] constant, by what factor does rate change in the same idealised empirical model?
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Pendulum graph: non-zero intercept is evidence
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: A teacher-written idealised T^2 versus length graph has points (0.20 m, 0.84 s2) and (0.80 m, 3.24 s2). The relation for a small-angle ideal pendulum is T^2=(4 pi2/g)L plus possible systematic offset.
tasks: Find the slope and vertical intercept.
Estimate g from the slope.
Explain why setting the graph intercept to zero by force could bias g.
marks: The intercept is 0.84 - (4.00 x 0.20) = 0.04 s2.
For the ideal small-angle model slope = 4 pi2/g.
The non-zero intercept may indicate systematic timing or length-offset effects.
A forced-origin line changes fitted gradient and therefore changes inferred g.
A short sampled interval and rounded measurements introduce uncertainty.
The model assumes suitably small amplitude and controlled timing.
questions.common_error: Treating a physically expected zero intercept as permission to erase a measured offset.
questions.transfer_question: Using a forced-origin slope of 4.05 s2 m-1 instead, calculate g.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Convex lens: separate image size from focal length
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: An ideal thin convex lens forms a real image of an object at u=0.300 m on the opposite side at v=0.600 m. Treat u and v as positive distances for this real-image thin-lens equation: 1/f=1/u+1/v.
tasks: Find the focal length.
Find the magnitude and orientation of the lateral magnification.
State why a single idealized measurement cannot prove the lens has exactly this focal length.
marks: Thus focal length f = 0.200 m.
Optical power P = 1/f = +5.00 dioptres.
Magnification magnitude |m| = v/u = 2.00.
The real image is inverted in this simplified configuration.
Sign conventions need to be explicitly defined, not mixed between equations.
Lens thickness, aberrations and distance-reading errors can affect real measurements.
One data pair has limited precision and cannot establish exact calibration or universal paraxial validity.
questions.common_error: Mixing signed-distance conventions and concluding upright real images in the simple convex-lens model.
questions.transfer_question: For the same ideal lens f=0.200 m and an object 0.400 m away, predict v.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Terminal-voltage model: gradient and prediction
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: An already-completed fictional cell dataset gives (I=0.100 A, V=1.49 V) and (I=0.400 A, V=1.37 V). Model V=E-Ir with E and r constant over the interval.
tasks: Calculate internal resistance and emf from the gradient and intercept.
Predict terminal voltage at I=0.250 A.
Explain one reason why an actual cell may depart from a perfect line.
marks: V=E-Ir implies gradient = -r.
Internal resistance r = 0.400 ohm.
A linear model assumes r and E fixed over the sampled interval.
Cell temperature and chemical state can change while current varies.
A two-point line does not quantify random measurement uncertainty or verify wider-range linearity.
questions.common_error: Taking the negative slope as a negative internal resistance.
questions.transfer_question: At I=0.500 A, predict V using the same hypothetical model.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Young modulus: unit conversions dominate
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: A hypothetical elastic steel-wire analysis uses original length L=2.00 m, diameter d=0.500 mm, force F=10.0 N and measured extension e=0.500 mm. Use a circular cross-section and linear elastic behavior; there is no setup instruction.
tasks: Find cross-sectional area in m2.
Estimate Young modulus in Pa.
Explain when doubling force might or might not double extension.
marks: Area A=pi r2 = 1.96 x 10^-7 m2.
Extension e=0.500 mm = 5.00 x 10^-4 m.
Young modulus Y=(F/A)/(e/L)=FL/(Ae).
Numerator FL = 20.0 N m.
Y approx 2.04 x 10^11 Pa.
In the linear elastic range, doubling force would approximately double extension at fixed geometry.
Beyond the proportional or elastic range the assumption may fail; data alone do not establish that a wire remains elastic indefinitely.
questions.common_error: Failing to convert mm to m and forgetting that cross-sectional area depends on diameter squared.
questions.transfer_question: If the measured wire diameter were actually 1.00 mm with other values unchanged, what is the revised Young modulus estimate?
questions.transfer_answer: One quarter of the original estimate: approximately 5.09 x 10^10 Pa, since A is proportional to d2.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.
